title: Isolated Downstream Validation and Single‑Repair Effects in Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study cand-003-stud-001) that isolates purely downstream deterministic validation plus a bounded single-repair intervention under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using 1,000 deterministic intents (1,000 paired episodes) drawn from a synthetic workflow stress corpus and a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; any paired outcome difference can therefore arise only from the validator decision and at most one permitted repair call (guarded arm). Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; discordants n10 = 5 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only); preregistered primary test exact two‑sided McNemar p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). Preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.001, 0.01]. Total hosted model calls recorded = 1005 (1000 shared initial + 5 repair). We present the exact McNemar as the confirmatory inference, the bootstrap interval as a preregistered descriptive summary, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, ceiling effects, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from operator intent to device configuration promises operational efficiency but raises safety risks: incorrect command ordering, transient invariant violations, and unauthorized touches of protected fields can convert plausible plans into damaging live changes. Prior empirical work documents frequent LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that reduce correctness in code- and config-like generation and motivates verifier‑augmented architectures that detect and sometimes repair unsafe outputs [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered paired experiment explicitly designed to isolate the incremental effect of a deterministic validator and a single bounded repair invocation when both experimental arms reuse the exact same initial sampled candidate (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). Our central empirical estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) computed on complete pairs. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics no first‑pass sampling differences exist between arms; therefore any paired outcome difference can only arise from the deterministic validator decision and the allowed at‑most‑one repair call. This causal framing differs from generate→validate→repair evaluations that mix validator effects with independent sampling or decoding changes and makes the estimand precisely: baseline single‑shot/initial validity versus final guarded‑pipeline validity after deterministic validation and permitted repair.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired confirmatory study (Npairs = 1,000) with deterministic task selection from a challenging synthetic NetOps workflow stress corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and explicit runtime configuration reporting (declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; model configuration recorded temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (3) Transparent reporting of the preregistered primary inference (exact two‑sided McNemar, p = 0.0625), the preregistered paired bootstrap descriptive summary (95% percentile CI = [0.001, 0.01], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an evidence‑grounded interpretation that accounts for sparse discordant counts, near‑unity baseline, and validator scope.
sections.related_work:
Work evaluating LLMs on structured generation and configuration tasks has converged on three observations relevant to our study. First, LLMs produce syntactic and semantic errors in structured domains (code, configs) and are sensitive to prompt and decoding choices; empirical surveys and controlled benchmarks document hallucination modes that materially affect downstream correctness [3],[4]. Second, approaches that pair generation with validation—ranging from schema/constrained decoding to separate deterministic validators and repair calls—are proposed and demonstrated to reduce observable errors in offline or synthetic settings, though measured gains depend strongly on validator coverage and benchmark design [5],[6],[7]. Third, agentic and multi‑stage NetOps architectures emphasize governance, auditability, and protocol‑mediated execution (proof‑carrying traces, canaries, rollbacks) as necessary complements to any single model’s behavior; these contributions provide architectural arguments and prototypes showing operational reliability depends on validator fidelity and orchestration policies [8],[9],[10].

Two points from the verified literature motivate our paired shared_initial_candidate design. Prior generate→validate→repair reports often conflate (a) downstream verification/repair with (b) independent first‑pass generation changes (prompting or decoding). When both mechanisms are active, attributing improvement to the validator alone is ambiguous. The literature therefore supports isolating downstream effects to understand validator/repair marginal returns prior to exploring end‑to‑end generator+validator interventions [5],[7]. Second, several method papers show constrained decoding increases executable outputs in structured tasks, but these results are often domain-specific (cheminformatics, clinical) and depend on strong schema tooling; transfer to multi‑device NetOps with dependency ordering and protected‑field constraints is nontrivial [11],[12]. Our study complements these lines by holding generation constant and measuring only the deterministic downstream effect of a validator plus a bounded single repair invocation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. The study preregistration (study id cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation and executed by a registered analysis executor. Core preregistered items used without deviation include: task_count = 1,000 complete pairs; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per task deterministically reused by both arms); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary confirmatory test = exact two‑sided McNemar. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 for descriptive summaries.

Task corpus and deterministic selection. Tasks derive from the synthetic challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus. The selection rule deterministically maps ordinal j ∈ [0,999] to fixed task indices, producing 1,000 unique intents. Each manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty annotations (levels include 'very_hard' and 'extreme'). Representative patterns in the corpus include multi‑step workflows such as failover_then_offline_reconfiguration, rolling_access_vlan_migration, safe_access_service_transfer, and composed_redundancy_and_access_maintenance; these patterns encode ordering and transient invariants that the validator checks.

Adapter, model configuration, and validator. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the declared provider/model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The recorded model_configuration shows temperature = null/unset; per preregistered reporting we explicitly note that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics); the guarded arm applies deterministic validator checks and may invoke at most one repair call if the validator rejects the initial candidate. The validator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, is a deterministic digital‑twin emulator that parses candidate command sequences and checks required command presence/order, protected‑field noninterference, and workflow invariants; it emits a binary safe‑deploy decision and structured traces documenting validation_before, repair_applied, and validation_after.

Causal semantics under shared_initial_candidate. Because the same initial candidate was reused by baseline and guarded episodes for every pair, any paired outcome difference can only arise from the deterministic validator decision and at most one permitted repair invocation. We therefore interpret the estimand strictly as: baseline single‑shot/initial validity versus final guarded‑pipeline validity after deterministic validation and permitted repair. The preregistration explicitly set independent_condition_generation = false; no independent first‑pass generations were executed for alternate prompt or decoding arms (those follow‑ups are proposed but were not part of the frozen execution). This design isolates downstream validator/repair marginal effects but precludes measuring generator‑level interventions.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 2,000; completed = 2,000; complete_pairs = 1,000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call audit shows hosted model call event count = 1,005 consisting of 1,000 shared initial generations and 5 repair invocations (stage counts recorded in the deterministic reconciliation artifact).

Primary paired outcomes (preregistered). The observed paired contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625; under the preregistered α = 0.05 this hypothesis is not supported.

Preregistered descriptive summary and seed‑ed bootstrap. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) computed by the registered executor is [0.001, 0.01]. This bootstrap CI is a preregistered descriptive summary and, in this run, excludes zero despite the confirmatory p‑value being >0.05. This outcome is consistent with known discrete behavior of exact paired tests when discordant counts are extremely sparse: bootstrap percentile bounds can omit zero while exact two‑sided tests remain nondiscovering because the discrete null distribution concentrates mass on symmetric small counts.

Repair mechanics and representative diagnostics. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred. Archived validator traces for repaired pairs document that the validator rejected the shared initial candidate for rule‑level violations (examples: required_sequence ordering errors and protected‑field touches), invoked a single repair call that produced a repaired candidate, and then revalidated the repaired candidate as acceptable. Representative task manifests and response traces in the artifact set show the repaired episodes are concentrated among higher difficulty patterns (annotated 'very_hard' or 'extreme') with multi‑step required_sequences. Total hosted model calls = 1,005 (1,000 shared initial + 5 repair) and all deterministic reconciliation checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive evidence. By the preregistered decision rule the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625) is the confirmatory outcome and does not reach two‑sided α = 0.05; we therefore do not claim confirmatory support for a nonzero paired increase under the prespecified two‑sided test. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a prespecified descriptive summary computed by the registered executor and is reported to aid interpretation; it does not override the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. A post‑hoc one‑sided McNemar (exploratory) gave p = 0.03125 and is explicitly labeled exploratory in the artifacts.

Interpretation given sparse discordants and ceiling effects. The preregistered power calculation assumed baseline≈0.60 and targeted an absolute increase of 0.15. Observed baseline = 0.995 is far higher than assumed; this concentrates mass in the concordant success cell (n11 = 995) and leaves only five discordant pairs. With n10 = 5 and n01 = 0 the exact two‑sided p = 0.0625 sits marginally above 0.05. The practical implication is that when baseline validity is near unity, detecting tiny absolute gains (here 0.005) requires either substantially larger paired sample sizes or a design that increases discordant prevalence (for example, independent generation arms, injected failures, or larger repair budgets). The observed bootstrap CI reflects sample‑level variability but, given the small discordant count, should be interpreted cautiously.

Failure‑mode diagnostics and difficulty patterns. Archived validator traces indicate the five repaired cases shared common, rule‑level failure modes: ordering violations in required_sequence and unauthorized touches of protected interfaces. Representative task manifests in the artifacts show these repaired tasks are drawn from complex multi‑step workflows (patterns cataloged as safe_access_service_transfer, failover_then_offline_reconfiguration, rolling_access_vlan_migration, and composed_redundancy_and_access_maintenance) and were annotated as 'very_hard' or 'extreme'. This pattern is consistent with the intuition that multi‑step dependency constraints increase ordering vulnerabilities. However, only five repairs occurred, limiting inference about repair efficacy across the full failure modality spectrum; observed evidence is compatible with (a) low prevalence of validator‑detectable violations in the sampled corpus, (b) generator behavior producing largely valid initial candidates for the declared model+prompt, and/or (c) validator coverage that does not capture some semantic error classes.

Design rationale and scope. The shared_initial_candidate paired design intentionally isolates downstream validator and single‑repair effects and avoids conflation with prompt/decoding or sampling interventions. This yields a precise causal estimand (baseline initial validity versus final guarded validity after deterministic validation and up to one repair) but precludes measuring effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompt engineering. The preregistration planned follow‑ups to address those broader estimands; we reiterate that those arms were not executed here under shared_initial_candidate.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows that verifier‑guided single repairs can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but marginal gains are small when baseline validity is already near unity and when the repair budget is highly constrained. Supported, concrete follow‑ups include: (1) executing independent first‑pass generation arms to measure generator+validator interactions (preregistered but not run here under shared_initial_candidate); (2) sweeping repair budgets (0..k repairs) to quantify marginal returns per additional repair call; (3) expanding validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity; and (4) evaluating multiple model families. Each follow‑up should prespecify baseline failure ranges and adjust power calculations to the expected operating regime.

Threats to validity. Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary reflects deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate downstream effects but prevent measuring first‑pass generation interventions. External validity: synthetic corpus and single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization to heterogeneous production environments. Conclusion validity: extreme baseline success produced sparse discordant counts and discrete p‑value behavior, reducing sensitivity for small absolute effects. These limitations were identified in the preregistration and are documented in the archived manifest.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar did not meet two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total hosted model calls recorded = 1,005. The preregistered confirmatory result is the exact McNemar outcome; the paired bootstrap CI and one‑sided test are reported as descriptive and exploratory respectively. Artifact‑grounded evidence indicates downstream validator/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes in structured NetOps workflows, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budgets, validator coverage, and model families are necessary to map marginal returns in realistic operating regimes.

Orchestration and validator: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the validator/digital twin. Preregistration: study cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls and recorded in the archived execution manifest). Human role and autonomy boundary: after the autonomy lock the research run executed the preregistered experiment, analysis, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
